name: The Catalpa of the Van Abbemuseum
age_estimate: around a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.neighbourhood: Eindhoven city centre, on the Dommel beside the Van Abbemuseum

access: Free. Public green strip (plantsoen) beside the museum's main entrance, open at all times.
transport: Eindhoven Centraal, about 15 minutes on foot south along the Dommel, or bus to the Van Abbemuseum stop.
story:
Nobody can say whether this catalpa or the museum beside it came first. The national tree register puts its planting between 1900 and 1910. Eindhoven's own tree database, refreshed this month, records 1930. Both are official, both list the tree as monumental, and the gap between them is a generation. It matters here, because the Van Abbemuseum went up in 1936, built by A.J. Kropholler for the cigar manufacturer Henri van Abbe to hold his collection. On the register's dating the tree was already thirty years old and watched the building arrive on its doorstep. On the city's dating it went in six years before the builders did. We have not picked a winner between the two.

What is not in dispute: this is a southern catalpa of fifteen to eighteen metres, on the public green strip between the museum and the Dommel, and it is not alone. Four more catalpas stand within thirty five metres, all of them carrying the same monumental rating in the city's records. Catalpa comes from the southeastern United States, and it keeps American hours: it is one of the last trees in a Dutch park to come into leaf, so in April this corner still looks bare while everything around it has gone green. By July the crown is full of white flowers marked in yellow and purple.

If you know when these were planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad heart-shaped leaves, which appear weeks later than anything around them, and by its height of fifteen to eighteen metres. It stands on the green strip between the Van Abbemuseum and the Dommel.

best_time.label: July, when the white flowers open across the crown

name: The Cedar of Pastoor Sickingstraat
access: Free. Stands in a paved urban street setting, visible from the public street at all times.
transport: About 1.7 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal (Joriskwartier, Stratum); bus lines serve nearby Aalsterweg, or about 20 minutes on foot.
story:
Eindhoven's own tree database contradicts itself about this tree. One field of the record calls it a blue Atlas cedar. Another field in the same record gives the species as Cedrus libani, the cedar of Lebanon, which is what the national register calls it as well. The two registers point at the same spot, less than three metres apart, so this is one tree wearing two labels rather than two trees. The species are close relatives and genuinely hard to tell apart: both hold their branches out flat in layers, both carry short needles in tufts, and it is the cones and the needle detail that settle the question. We have listed it as the cedar of Lebanon because two of the three entries say so, and we are flagging the disagreement rather than tidying it away. If you can settle it standing underneath, tell us.

The rest is plainer. The city dates the planting to 1930, which puts the tree at about ninety-five years, and records it at fifteen to eighteen metres. The national register lists its history as unknown, which is a register's way of saying nobody ever wrote anything down about it.

Its surroundings are far younger than it is. The Joriskwartier went up mostly around 2006, by which time this cedar had been standing for some seventy-five years. It now holds a layered evergreen crown over a paved street, in a neighbourhood built around it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches held out flat in layers and the short blue-green needles in tufts, a cedar of fifteen to eighteen metres. It stands on the Pastoor Sickingstraat, in paving rather than grass.

name: The Honey Locust of the Stadspaviljoen
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan 1, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
story:
This honey locust stands more than twenty-four metres tall, which the species almost never manages in the Netherlands. Gleditsia triacanthos is an American tree from the Mississippi basin, planted in European cities for its fine feathery leaflets and its indifference to bad air, and it usually stops well short of that height here. Eindhoven's tree survey files this one in its top band, above twenty-four metres. The national register lists it on dendrological grounds, which is a register saying the tree earns its protection for what it is rather than for anything that happened to it.

Its age is disputed. The register bands the planting between 1890 and 1900, which would make it about 130 years old. The city's record says 1940, which would make it 86. Nobody has reconciled the two and we are not going to pick one for them.

It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, once the coach house of Landgoed Den Elzent. The tobacco manufacturer H.F.C. Coolen sold that estate in 1876 to the Amsterdam merchant B.H.A. Sinkel, who had Leonard Springer lay the grounds out as a landscape garden. Eindhoven opened them to the public in 1921 and named the place Stadswandelpark ten years later. The corner is a group rather than a single specimen: beeches, pin oaks, black locusts and a sweet chestnut a few steps away, all of them monumental in the city's records.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fine feathery leaflets, small for a tree of its size, and by its height of over twenty-four metres. It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen in the Stadswandelpark, near a sweet chestnut.

best_time.label: October, when the small leaflets turn clear yellow and come down early

name: The Sweet Chestnut of the Stadspaviljoen
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
story:
Two registers place this chestnut within eighty centimetres of each other and disagree about its age by fifty years. The national register bands the planting 1890 to 1900. Eindhoven's own tree database says 1940. The position is settled and the age is not, which is the usual shape of these things: somebody once stood under the tree with a GPS, and nobody ever counted anything.

The species is not in dispute. A sweet chestnut in a Dutch park is a food tree that stopped being used as one. Castanea sativa came north with the Romans, who ground the nuts into flour, and it fed people across southern Europe for centuries afterwards. This one reaches fifteen to eighteen metres, hangs cream catkins in July, and in October drops spiny burrs into the grass, where the squirrels reach them first.

It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, a few dozen metres from the honey locust, which makes the pair one short walk rather than two separate errands. The pavilion was the coach house of Landgoed Den Elzent, a private country estate on the edge of town until Eindhoven opened the grounds to the public in 1921. The trees in this corner are a set rather than a scatter: beeches, pin oaks and black locusts, all of them monumental in the city's records, dated by the city to 1910 and 1940.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long leaves with saw-toothed edges and, in autumn, by the spiny husks lying in the grass under it. It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, a few dozen metres from the much taller honey locust.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny burrs split and the chestnuts come down

name: The Plane of Marienhage
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Kanaalstraat 6, behind the former Marienhage monastery, Eindhoven
location.neighbourhood: Eindhoven city centre, on the Dommel

access: Free; the LRMB register lists it as visitable, but it is not visible from the street. It stands behind the former Marienhage monastery (now a hotel, DomusDELA/Hotel Marienhage) against the Dommel; reach it via the public Dommelpad riverside walking route, which is documented as passing this exact site (Marienhage is a marked stage point of the long-distance 'Ons Kloosterpad' trail).
transport: Eindhoven Centraal, about 10 minutes on foot, near Kanaalstraat / the Dommel.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely on location (4.8m apart): the national LRMB register (nr 1690274, planted_band 1880-1890, reason 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=nee) and the Gemeente Eindhoven open-data 'bomen' dataset (species Platanus hispanica, status_ter_indicatie 'Monumentaal', plantjaar 1935, hoogte '>24 m'), current as of the dataset's 2026-09-07 refresh (good 'alive now' evidence). AGE CONFLICT: register implies planted 1880-1890 (about 136-146 years old today), municipal record says 1935 (about 91 years old); no winner picked, both reported; either way this is a large (>24m) old specimen. ACCESS CAVEAT, flag for the writer/curator: the register itself marks 'visible: nee', meaning it cannot be seen from the public street, and the site (Klooster Marienhage, founded 1419 for Augustinian hermits, rebuilt after 1876/1890, sold 2017) is now a boutique hotel/DomusDELA. A web search found the redevelopment plan explicitly making 'the garden... public' with a new bridge over the Dommel, and Marienhage is listed as a marked point on the long-distance Dommelpad/Ons Kloosterpad walking route, which is reasonable evidence of a public path reaching the riverside behind the building, but this pass could not directly confirm on the ground (no OSM check run, no site photo seen) whether that path currently passes within sight of this specific tree or whether it crosses hotel-controlled grounds. Checked per the Ypres technique in BRIEF_RESEARCH.md: an Overpass query within 60m of the tree's coordinate found several `highway=footway`/`highway=pedestrian` ways with paving-stone or sett surfaces and a `leisure=garden` area, none tagged `access=private` or otherwise restricted; this is supporting evidence (not proof) that the riverside grounds behind Kanaalstraat 6 carry public paths rather than being sealed off, consistent with the redevelopment plan's own claim that the garden was being made public. No girth or diameter figure found in either source.
